chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.text:
## How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
Published/updated: 2026-08-19
An oven can look fine from the outside while the inside tells a very different story. Grease splatters collect around the walls, crumbs burn onto the bottom, and old food residue can turn into a stubborn layer that seems impossible to remove.
If you prefer to avoid strong commercial oven cleaners, you have several gentler options. Baking soda, warm water, dish soap, and a little patience can handle a surprising amount of everyday buildup. Vinegar can also help in specific situations, but it works best as a follow-up rather than a magic ingredient that does all the work.
The right method depends on the oven, the type of mess, and whether your oven has a self-cleaning or steam-cleaning function. This guide explains how to clean an oven naturally, what actually works, what to avoid, and how to keep the oven from becoming a major project again.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: Before You Clean: Check Your Oven Manual
chunks.text:
## Before You Clean: Check Your Oven Manual
Before putting any homemade cleaner inside your oven, check the manufacturer’s instructions.
Different ovens use different interior coatings. Some have special finishes that should not be scrubbed with abrasive materials. Self-cleaning ovens also require specific precautions, and some manufacturers recommend against using certain cleaners before or after a self-cleaning cycle.
If your oven manual says not to use baking soda, vinegar, steam, or another product on a particular surface, follow the manufacturer’s instructions instead.
Also make sure the oven is completely cool before you begin.
## What You Need for Natural Oven Cleaning
A simple setup is enough for most routine oven messes:
- Baking soda
- Warm water
- Mild dish soap
- White vinegar in a spray bottle, if appropriate for your oven
- Microfiber cloths
- A non-scratch sponge
- A soft scrub brush
- An old toothbrush for corners
- A plastic scraper for stubborn residue
- Towels to protect the floor
Avoid metal blades, steel wool, and rough scouring pads unless the appliance manufacturer specifically allows them.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: How to Clean an Oven Naturally With Baking Soda
chunks.text:
## How to Clean an Oven Naturally With Baking Soda
Baking soda is useful because it is mildly abrasive and can help loosen greasy residue without relying on a harsh oven-cleaning formula.
## Step 1: Remove the Racks
Take out all oven racks and set them aside.
This gives you room to work and prevents you from accidentally getting cleaner on the racks while scrubbing the walls.
## Step 2: Remove Loose Debris
Use a dry cloth, soft brush, or handheld vacuum to remove crumbs and loose burnt food.
Do not skip this step. It is much easier to deal with baked-on grease when loose debris is already gone.
## Step 3: Make a Baking Soda Paste
Mix baking soda with enough warm water to create a spreadable paste.
You want something thick enough to cling to the oven surface. It should not be watery.
For greasy areas, a few drops of dish soap can be added to the paste. Dish soap helps break down oils while the baking soda provides gentle scrubbing action.
## Step 4: Apply the Paste
Spread the paste over the dirty areas of the oven interior.
Avoid heating elements, vents, light fixtures, and other components that the manufacturer says should not be coated with cleaning products.
You do not need to cover every square inch if only certain areas are dirty. Concentrate on the bottom, side walls, and spots with visible grease.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.text:
## Step 5: Let It Sit
This is the part people often rush.
Give the paste several hours to work. For heavy buildup, leaving it overnight can make the next step much easier.
The goal is to soften and loosen the residue so you do not have to attack it with force.
## Step 6: Wipe and Scrub Gently
Use a damp microfiber cloth or non-scratch sponge to remove the paste.
Work in small sections. If a spot does not come clean immediately, re-wet it and give it more time rather than using excessive pressure.
A soft brush or old toothbrush can help around corners and seams.
## Step 7: Rinse Thoroughly
Once the baking soda paste and grease are gone, wipe the interior several times with clean water.
Baking soda residue can leave a white film if it is not fully removed. Use clean, damp microfiber cloths until the surface feels clean rather than powdery.
## Step 8: Dry the Interior
Leave the oven door open for a while so the interior can dry completely.
Before using the oven again, make sure no cleaner or loose residue remains.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: Can You Clean an Oven With Vinegar and Baking Soda?
chunks.text:
## Can You Clean an Oven With Vinegar and Baking Soda?
Yes, but the two ingredients are often misunderstood.
When vinegar and baking soda are mixed together, they react and fizz. That reaction looks impressive, but much of the cleaning power is simply the result of the acid and base neutralizing each other.
A better approach is to use them separately when appropriate.
Start with baking soda paste to loosen grease. Once you have wiped most of it away, a light spray of diluted vinegar can help lift remaining alkaline residue. Then wipe the surface with clean water.
Do not rely on vinegar to dissolve years of baked-on grease by itself.
Also never mix vinegar with bleach or other incompatible cleaning chemicals.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: How to Clean Oven Glass Naturally
chunks.text:
## How to Clean Oven Glass Naturally
The glass door is often the most noticeable part of a dirty oven.
Start by making a thin baking soda paste with water. Spread it over the glass and let it sit for about 15 to 30 minutes.
Use a soft sponge or microfiber cloth to loosen the residue. For a stubborn spot, a plastic scraper can help if your manufacturer’s instructions allow it.
Wipe the glass clean with a damp cloth, then dry it with a clean microfiber towel.
Avoid using abrasive powders or metal scrubbers. Scratches on oven glass are not worth the risk.
If grease has collected between the panes of glass, do not disassemble the door unless the manufacturer’s instructions specifically explain how to do it. Many oven doors contain springs, hinges, and seals that can be difficult to reinstall correctly.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.text:
## How to Clean Oven Racks
Oven racks often need more soaking than scrubbing.
Place the racks in a bathtub, large plastic container, or another safe area that can handle water. Protect the surface if needed.
Soak the racks in warm water with dish soap. Give the residue time to soften.
After soaking, use a non-scratch sponge to remove the loosened grime. A soft brush can help around corners.
Rinse the racks thoroughly and dry them completely before putting them back into the oven.
Do not use a harsh abrasive on racks with a special finish. If the racks have become difficult to slide, check the manufacturer’s care instructions before applying oil or other products.
## How to Clean a Gas Oven Naturally
Gas ovens need a little extra attention around burners and vents.
First, make sure the oven is off and completely cool. Do not allow liquid or cleaning paste to enter burner openings.
Remove loose crumbs with a soft brush or vacuum. Clean removable components according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
For the oven cavity, the baking soda paste method can work well for ordinary grease. Apply it only to areas that are safe to clean and keep it away from gas ports.
If you are unsure about a burner component or gas connection, do not experiment with it. Leave the component alone and consult the appliance manual or a qualified technician.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: How to Clean an Electric Oven Naturally
chunks.text:
## How to Clean an Electric Oven Naturally
Electric ovens also require care around heating elements.
Do not coat heating elements with baking soda paste or spray them with liquid unless your manufacturer’s instructions specifically permit it.
Instead, clean the oven walls and bottom carefully with a damp cloth or appropriate natural cleaner while avoiding the electrical components.
If a spill has baked onto the heating element itself, check the manual for the correct procedure. Some small residue burns away during normal use, while other situations require specific cleaning instructions.
## What About Self-Cleaning Ovens?
A self-cleaning oven uses very high temperatures to burn off food residue.
That does not mean you should automatically use the self-cleaning cycle for every cleaning job. The process can produce smoke and odors, and the manufacturer may recommend specific preparation steps.
If you use the self-cleaning function:
- Remove pans, racks, and items the manual says to remove.
- Wipe out loose crumbs first.
- Keep the kitchen ventilated.
- Stay nearby while the cycle is running.
- Follow the manufacturer’s instructions exactly.
Do not use additional cleaning chemicals inside the oven before running a self-cleaning cycle unless the manufacturer specifically says you can.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.text:
## What About Steam Cleaning?
Some newer ovens include a steam-cleaning function. Steam can be useful for fresh or lighter spills because moisture softens residue.
If your oven has a steam-clean setting, use it according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
If it does not, do not assume that placing any container of water inside a hot oven is automatically safe. Containers can crack, steam can cause burns, and the wrong method can damage an appliance.
Natural cleaning should never mean ignoring safety instructions.
## How to Remove Burnt Food From the Bottom of an Oven
Burnt food needs patience more than force.
First remove loose pieces with a plastic scraper if permitted by the manufacturer.
Then apply a baking soda paste to the affected area and let it sit for several hours. Wipe away what has softened and repeat if necessary.
For very thick carbonized buildup, several gentle treatments are safer than one aggressive scrubbing session.
If the bottom of the oven has a special coating, follow the care instructions rather than using an abrasive scraper.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: How to Remove Grease From Oven Walls
chunks.text:
## How to Remove Grease From Oven Walls
Grease responds well to dish soap because soap helps break down oils.
Add a few drops of mild dish soap to warm water and use a microfiber cloth or soft sponge. For heavier grease, follow with a baking soda paste.
Work from the top down so loosened residue does not run over areas you have already cleaned.
Rinse with clean water afterward. Leaving cleaner behind can create odors the next time you heat the oven.
## Natural Oven Cleaning Mistakes to Avoid
## Using Too Much Water
An oven is not a surface you should soak. Excess liquid can enter vents, electrical components, or other areas that should remain dry.
## Scrubbing Too Hard
If residue is not coming off, give the cleaner more time. Excessive pressure can damage coatings.
## Mixing Cleaning Chemicals
Natural products are not automatically safe when mixed. Never combine bleach with vinegar, ammonia, or other incompatible cleaners.
## Cleaning a Hot Oven
Heat can make fumes stronger and can cause burns. Start with a completely cool oven.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.text:
## Ignoring the Manufacturer’s Instructions
A natural cleaner is not universally safe for every oven. The appliance manual should always take priority.
## How Often Should You Clean Your Oven?
There is no single schedule that works for every household.
If you cook frequently, inspect the oven every few weeks. Wipe up fresh spills once the oven is cool rather than waiting for them to burn onto the surface.
A more complete cleaning every few months is a reasonable starting point for many homes. Heavy cooking, roasting, baking, and frequent spills may require more attention.
If you notice smoke from old residue, persistent odors, or visible grease on the interior, it is time for a cleaning.
## A Simple Maintenance Routine
You can prevent a deep oven clean from becoming a full-day project.
After a spill, let the oven cool and wipe it before the residue hardens.
Once a week, check the bottom and oven door for crumbs and grease.
Every few weeks, wipe the accessible interior surfaces.
Every few months, give the oven a more thorough clean based on its condition.

chunks.section: When DIY Oven Cleaning Is Not Enough
chunks.text:
## When DIY Oven Cleaning Is Not Enough
There is a point where repeated DIY cleaning becomes less practical.
If an oven has years of heavy grease, extensive baked-on carbon, or a large amount of residue across multiple surfaces, getting it back to a clean baseline can take significant time.
Professional cleaning can be useful when you are preparing for a move, getting ready to host a major event, or resetting a home after a long period without a deep clean.
SHINENOS can handle the broader kitchen cleaning around the oven as part of a professional deep clean, so you are not spending an entire weekend working through appliances, cabinets, counters, floors, and bathrooms one task at a time.
## Frequently Asked Questions
## What is the best natural cleaner for an oven?
For many ovens, a baking soda and water paste is a practical natural option for loosening grease and baked-on residue. Always check the manufacturer’s instructions before using it.
## Can I use vinegar to clean my oven?
Vinegar can help remove residue and odors, but it is not usually strong enough to handle heavy baked-on grease by itself. Use it only when appropriate for your oven’s materials and care instructions.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.section: How long should baking soda sit in an oven?
chunks.text:
## How long should baking soda sit in an oven?
For light buildup, 15 to 30 minutes may help. Heavy grease can benefit from several hours or an overnight application, provided the method is safe for the oven’s interior finish.
## Can I use baking soda on the oven glass?
Baking soda can work on many oven glass surfaces, but avoid aggressive scrubbing. Check your appliance instructions first and use a soft cloth or sponge.
## How do I clean an oven without chemicals?
You can use simple ingredients such as baking soda, water, and mild dish soap for many routine cleaning tasks. “Natural” does not mean every surface can be treated the same way, so always check the appliance manual.
## How do I stop my oven from smelling after cleaning?
Rinse the interior thoroughly and allow it to dry. Any leftover cleaner or baking soda can create an odor when heated. If the smell continues, check for hidden grease or residue.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean an Oven Naturally (Every Method, Every Oven Type)
chunks.text:
## Final Takeaway
Learning how to clean an oven naturally is mostly about using a gentle method and giving the cleaner enough time to work. Baking soda can loosen grease, dish soap can break down oily residue, and careful wiping can remove the mess without relying on harsh products.
The key is not to rush. Protect the heating elements and vents, avoid abrasive tools, follow your oven manufacturer’s instructions, and clean small spills before they become baked-on problems.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.text:
## How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
Published/updated: 2026-08-19
Stainless steel appliances look great when they are clean, but they have a frustrating habit of showing every fingerprint, water spot, greasy smudge, and streak. A refrigerator can be spotless inside and still make the whole kitchen look messy because the front is covered in marks.
The good news is that stainless steel does not need a complicated cleaning routine. The biggest difference comes from using a soft cloth, the right amount of moisture, and a technique that follows the grain of the metal. The wrong cleaner or an abrasive scrubber can leave scratches, dull patches, or a cloudy film that is harder to remove than the original dirt.
This guide explains how to clean stainless steel appliances safely, how to get a streak-free finish, what to use on fingerprints and grease, and which common cleaning habits can damage the surface.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: Why Stainless Steel Gets Streaky So Easily
chunks.text:
## Why Stainless Steel Gets Streaky So Easily
Stainless steel is not difficult to clean because the material is inherently dirty. It is difficult because the finish makes residue visible.
Cooking oils can settle on refrigerator doors, dishwashers, ranges, and microwave fronts. Hands leave natural oils behind every time someone opens a door or drawer. Water droplets can dry into mineral spots. Even a small amount of leftover cleaner can create a hazy layer that looks like more dirt.
The brushed finish also matters. Most stainless steel appliances have a visible grain, usually running horizontally or vertically. Wiping across that grain can make streaks more obvious and may trap residue in the texture.
The simplest rule is this: clean with the grain, use less product than you think you need, and finish with a dry microfiber cloth.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: What You Need to Clean Stainless Steel
chunks.text:
## What You Need to Clean Stainless Steel
You do not need a cabinet full of specialty products. For routine cleaning, gather:
- Two or three clean microfiber cloths
- Warm water
- A few drops of mild dish soap
- A soft, non-scratch sponge for heavier residue
- A dry microfiber cloth for polishing
- A stainless steel cleaner, if needed for your appliance finish
Keep a separate cloth for the final buffing step. If the cloth you use for cleaning is damp or already holding grease, it will usually leave the surface looking dull.
Before using any product, check the appliance manufacturer’s care instructions. Stainless steel finishes vary, and some appliances have a protective coating that requires specific cleaning methods.
## How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Step by Step
## Step 1: Remove Loose Dust and Crumbs
Start with a dry microfiber cloth. Wipe away crumbs, dust, and loose debris before adding water.
This small step matters because rubbing loose grit across a metal surface can create fine scratches. It also keeps dry debris from turning into a muddy film once you start wiping.
For refrigerator handles and the edges around doors, take a few extra seconds to remove dust that has collected in seams.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: Step 2: Mix a Mild Cleaning Solution
chunks.text:
## Step 2: Mix a Mild Cleaning Solution
For everyday dirt, warm water with a few drops of mild dish soap is usually enough.
You do not need a bucket filled with suds. Too much soap leaves more residue behind, which means more work during the final wipe.
If the appliance is only lightly dusty, plain warm water may be all you need.
## Step 3: Wipe With the Grain
Dampen a microfiber cloth and wring it out well. It should be moist, not dripping.
Look closely at the stainless steel and identify the direction of the grain. Wipe in that same direction using long, gentle strokes.
Do not scrub back and forth randomly. If you have a refrigerator with horizontal grain, keep your strokes horizontal. If the grain is vertical, work vertically.
Pay extra attention to handles, around buttons, and along the bottom edge of doors. These areas collect more oils and grime than the middle of the panel.
## Step 4: Rinse Away Soap Residue
If you used dish soap, take a second microfiber cloth, dampen it with clean water, and wipe the surface again.
This step is easy to skip, but it is one of the best ways to prevent streaks. Soap residue can dry into a hazy film that makes a clean appliance look dirty.
Use a clean cloth rather than the same one used to remove grease.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.text:
## Step 5: Dry and Buff
Finish with a dry microfiber cloth. Again, follow the grain.
Use light pressure and keep moving until the surface is dry. Do not leave water sitting on the appliance. This is especially important if your home has hard water because mineral deposits can become visible as the droplets dry.
A final dry buff often makes more difference than adding another cleaning product.
## How to Remove Fingerprints From Stainless Steel
Fingerprints are one of the most common complaints with stainless steel refrigerators and dishwashers.
For a few fresh fingerprints, start with a clean microfiber cloth slightly dampened with warm water. Wipe with the grain and then dry the surface.
For oily fingerprints, add a tiny amount of dish soap to warm water. Wipe the affected area, rinse with a clean damp cloth, and dry.
If fingerprints keep coming back immediately, the problem may not be the cleaning method. High-touch handles naturally need more frequent attention. A quick daily wipe of the handle area can keep the entire appliance looking cleaner without requiring a full cleaning every time.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: How to Clean Grease From Stainless Steel
chunks.text:
## How to Clean Grease From Stainless Steel
Kitchen grease is more stubborn than fingerprints because it can combine with dust and form a sticky film.
Start with warm water and a few drops of dish soap. Let the damp cloth sit against the greasy area for several seconds rather than immediately scrubbing. This gives the soap time to loosen the residue.
Wipe gently with the grain. If the grease remains, repeat the process instead of reaching immediately for an abrasive pad.
For heavier buildup, use a stainless steel-safe cleaner that is approved for your appliance. Always follow the product directions and test it on an inconspicuous area if you have not used it before.
Avoid aggressive scrubbing. Stainless steel can resist corrosion, but the finish can still be scratched or dulled.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: Can You Use Vinegar on Stainless Steel?
chunks.text:
## Can You Use Vinegar on Stainless Steel?
Vinegar is popular as a household cleaner, but it is not automatically the best choice for every stainless steel appliance.
Some stainless steel cleaning methods use diluted vinegar for mineral deposits or fingerprints. However, manufacturers can have different recommendations, and some appliance finishes include coatings that should not be treated with acidic cleaners.
If your manufacturer allows vinegar, use it sparingly and dilute it appropriately. Never let it sit on the surface for a long time. Wipe the surface clean afterward and dry it completely.
If you are unsure, mild dish soap and water is the safer starting point for routine cleaning.
## What About Olive Oil for Shine?
You may have seen the suggestion to wipe stainless steel with olive oil after cleaning.
It can create a temporary shine, but it can also leave an oily film that attracts dust and fingerprints. That may be especially annoying on refrigerator doors and dishwashers that are touched throughout the day.
If your appliance manufacturer recommends a stainless steel polish or conditioner, follow those instructions instead. The goal should be a clean surface, not a layer of oil that makes the appliance look shiny for a few hours.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: Cleaning Stainless Steel Pans and Cookware
chunks.text:
## Cleaning Stainless Steel Pans and Cookware
Stainless steel cookware needs a slightly different approach because food can become baked onto the cooking surface.
Let the pan cool before cleaning it. Add warm water and a small amount of dish soap, then allow it to soak if food is stuck.
For stubborn residue, use a non-scratch sponge and work gradually. A paste made from baking soda and water can help with some stuck-on food, but do not use aggressive abrasive pads that can scratch the surface.
For discoloration or mineral marks, a stainless steel-safe cleaner may be appropriate. Always follow the cookware manufacturer’s instructions.
Do not pour cold water into an extremely hot pan. The sudden temperature change can damage the cookware and can also create a safety hazard from steam.
## How to Clean Different Stainless Steel Appliances
## Refrigerator
Refrigerator doors usually need frequent fingerprint removal. Clean the handles first because they have the highest contact with hands. Then wipe the larger panels with the grain.
Check the bottom edges and around the door seals for crumbs and sticky residue.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.text:
## Dishwasher
The front panel can collect fingerprints, food splashes, and water spots. Wipe it after cleaning the kitchen, especially around the handle and control panel.
Avoid spraying cleaner directly onto buttons or electronic controls. Put the cleaner on the cloth instead.
## Oven and Range
Grease buildup is common around ranges. Clean splashes once the surface is cool rather than allowing grease to harden for days.
Do not assume the stainless steel exterior can be treated with the same cleaner used inside the oven. Oven cleaners can be harsh and may damage stainless steel finishes.
## Microwave
Wipe the exterior with a damp microfiber cloth and mild dish soap. Pay attention to the handle and areas around the buttons.
Keep liquid away from openings, seams, and electronic controls.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: What Not to Use on Stainless Steel
chunks.text:
## What Not to Use on Stainless Steel
Some cleaning shortcuts can permanently change the appearance of the surface.
Avoid:
- Steel wool
- Rough scouring pads
- Abrasive powders
- Strong bleach-based cleaners unless specifically approved by the manufacturer
- Glass cleaners unless the appliance manufacturer says they are safe
- Excessive amounts of cleaner
- Leaving acidic products sitting on the surface
- Scrubbing against the grain
- Spraying liquid directly into electronic controls
If a product says it is abrasive, be cautious. A cleaner can remove grime effectively while also leaving tiny scratches behind.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: How to Keep Stainless Steel Cleaner for Longer
chunks.text:
## How to Keep Stainless Steel Cleaner for Longer
The easiest way to clean stainless steel is to prevent heavy buildup.
Wipe fingerprints when you notice them rather than waiting until the entire door is covered. Clean cooking splashes soon after they happen. Dry water spots instead of letting them sit. Keep a microfiber cloth in a convenient kitchen drawer so a quick wipe does not become a project.
For busy households, a simple routine works well:
- Quick handle wipe as needed
- Appliance exterior wipe once or twice a week
- Deeper cleaning whenever grease, residue, or water spots build up
- Immediate cleanup of spills and splashes
If you already have a regular home cleaning routine, stainless steel appliances can be handled as part of that schedule. SHINENOS offers for homeowners who want routine cleaning handled consistently rather than saved for the weekend. recurring cleaning services
## Common Stainless Steel Cleaning Mistakes
## Using Too Much Product
More cleaner does not mean a cleaner surface. Excess product is one of the fastest ways to create a sticky or cloudy finish.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: Using Paper Towels for Heavy Scrubbing
chunks.text:
## Using Paper Towels for Heavy Scrubbing
Paper towels can work for light wiping, but a quality microfiber cloth is usually better for stainless steel because it picks up residue without leaving as much lint.
## Cleaning Across the Grain
This is a common reason a surface looks streaky even after the dirt is gone.
## Forgetting to Dry
Water left behind can create visible spots, particularly in areas with mineral-heavy water.
## Cleaning With a Dirty Cloth
A cloth that was just used on a greasy stovetop can spread oil around your refrigerator. Use clean microfiber cloths and change them when they become visibly dirty.
## When Professional Cleaning Makes Sense
Stainless steel is usually easy to maintain, but it is only one part of a kitchen. Grease also collects on cabinet doors, backsplashes, baseboards, appliance edges, and other surfaces that are easy to overlook.
If your kitchen needs more than a quick wipe-down, a professional can handle the larger reset while you maintain the appliances between visits. chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.text:
## Frequently Asked Questions
## What is the best thing to clean stainless steel appliances with?
For routine cleaning, warm water, a few drops of mild dish soap, and a soft microfiber cloth are a good starting point. Use a stainless steel-specific product when needed and follow the appliance manufacturer’s care instructions.
## How do you clean stainless steel without leaving streaks?
Use a small amount of cleaner, wipe with the grain, remove any soap residue with a clean damp cloth, and finish with a dry microfiber cloth. Too much product is a common cause of streaks.
## Can I use baking soda on stainless steel?
Baking soda can be useful for some stainless steel cookware and stubborn residue, but it can be mildly abrasive. Use it gently and avoid aggressive scrubbing, especially on decorative appliance finishes.
## How often should stainless steel appliances be cleaned?
High-touch areas such as handles may need cleaning several times a week. For most homes, a more complete exterior cleaning once a week is a practical starting point.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Stainless Steel Appliances Without Streaks or Scratches
chunks.section: How do I get fingerprints off stainless steel?
chunks.text:
## How do I get fingerprints off stainless steel?
Use a damp microfiber cloth for light fingerprints. For oily marks, use warm water with a few drops of mild dish soap, then rinse with a clean damp cloth and dry with a microfiber towel.
## Why does my stainless steel look cloudy after cleaning?
Cloudiness is often caused by leftover cleaner, soap residue, mineral deposits, or an oily polish. Re-clean the surface with mild soap and water, rinse, and dry thoroughly.
## Final Takeaway
Cleaning stainless steel appliances does not have to involve a collection of specialty products or aggressive scrubbing. Start gently, follow the grain, keep moisture controlled, and always finish with a dry microfiber cloth.
The best results usually come from consistency. A quick wipe of fingerprints and cooking splashes prevents the buildup that makes stainless steel much harder to clean later.

## Vacation Rental Cleaning: A Complete Guide for Airbnb Hosts in Minnesota
Published/updated: 2026-07-16
Running a successful short-term rental in Minnesota depends on three things more than anything else: location, price, and cleanliness. You can’t easily change the first two. Cleanliness is entirely within your control, and it directly determines your reviews, your occupancy rate, and your income.
Guests booking Airbnb and VRBO properties in the Twin Cities area expect hotel-standard cleanliness. When they arrive and the property doesn’t meet that standard, they say so in reviews. A few poor cleanliness reviews can take a property from four-star to three-star and reduce bookings significantly. A consistent five-star cleanliness rating, on the other hand, builds the kind of review momentum that sustains high occupancy.
This guide covers exactly what guests expect, the complete vacation rental cleaning checklist, how to price cleaning fees appropriately, when to hire a professional Airbnb cleaning service versus doing it yourself, and what to look for in a short-term rental cleaning service in Minnesota.

chunks.title: Blog: Vacation Rental Cleaning: A Complete Guide for Airbnb Hosts in Minnesota

## Kitchen Turnover Checklist
- Wash all dishes left in the sink or dishwasher
- Check all cabinets for dishes left behind and wash them
- Wipe down all countertops thoroughly
- Clean the inside of the microwave
- Clean the stovetop including burners and grates
- Wipe appliance exteriors (refrigerator, microwave, dishwasher, coffee maker)
- Check inside the refrigerator and remove any food left by guests
- Clean the refrigerator interior if needed
- Clean the sink and polish the faucet
- Empty and clean the trash can, replace the liner
- Sweep and mop the floor

## Bathroom Turnover Checklist
- Replace all towels with fresh, clean sets
- Scrub the toilet bowl, seat, exterior, and base
- Clean the sink and faucet
- Clean the shower or tub, removing any soap or product residue
- Wipe shower glass or clean the curtain liner
- Clean the mirror
- Mop the floor
- Empty the trash and replace the liner

chunks.title: Blog: Vacation Rental Cleaning: A Complete Guide for Airbnb Hosts in Minnesota
chunks.text:
## Bedroom Turnover Checklist
- Strip the bed completely and replace with fresh sheets, pillowcases, and duvet cover

- Dust all bedroom surfaces
- Vacuum the floor and under the bed
- Check closets and drawers for items left by guests
- Ensure adequate hangers are in the closet
- Check any lamps and nightstand items
## Living Areas Turnover Checklist
- Vacuum all sofas, chairs, and rugs
- Wipe down all hard surfaces: coffee table, side tables, TV stand

- Wipe down remotes with a disinfecting cloth
- Check all decorative items for dust or fingerprints

- Wipe down the entry table and coat hooks
- Clean interior of windows showing visible smudges

- Wipe down doorknobs, light switches, and frequently touched surfaces throughout

chunks.title: Blog: Vacation Rental Cleaning: A Complete Guide for Airbnb Hosts in Minnesota
chunks.text:
## Outdoor Areas (If Applicable)
- Sweep porch, deck, or patio
- Wipe down outdoor furniture
- Check outdoor trash containers and empty if needed

- Walk through every room from a guest’s perspective
- Check how the property smells: fresh but not artificially scented
- Verify all essential supplies are stocked
- Check that all appliances are set correctly (thermostat, refrigerator, etc.)

## Commercial Cleaning vs. Janitorial Services: What Does Your Business Need?
Published/updated: 2026-07-16
Business owners searching for commercial cleaning often encounter two terms used almost interchangeably by cleaning companies: commercial cleaning and janitorial services. They’re related but not identical, and choosing the wrong one for your business type can mean either overpaying for services you don’t need or underbuying and getting a workspace that doesn’t meet your standards.
Understanding the actual difference, what each type of service covers, how they’re typically structured and priced, and which one fits your specific business situation makes the selection process significantly more straightforward.

chunks.title: Blog: Commercial Cleaning vs. Janitorial Services: What Does Your Business Need?
chunks.section: The Core Difference Between Commercial Cleaning and Janitorial Services
chunks.text:
## The Core Difference Between Commercial Cleaning and Janitorial Services
The fundamental distinction comes down to scope and frequency.
refer to ongoing, routine maintenance cleaning typically performed daily or several times per week. Janitors maintain a clean baseline throughout regular business operations. Think: daily trash removal, restroom restocking and cleaning, floor sweeping and mopping, wiping down surfaces, and keeping common areas presentable during business hours or after each day’s use. Janitorial services
generally refers to deeper, periodic cleaning performed less frequently, typically weekly, monthly, or seasonally. Commercial cleaning goes beyond daily maintenance to address buildup, deep clean surfaces, clean windows, strip and wax floors, clean carpets, and address the areas that daily janitorial work doesn’t reach. Commercial cleaning
In practice, many cleaning companies use both terms loosely, and many provide both services under one contract. The meaningful question is not which label to use but rather what specific services your business needs, how often it needs them, and what that scope actually covers.

chunks.title: Blog: Commercial Cleaning vs. Janitorial Services: What Does Your Business Need?
chunks.text:
## What Janitorial Services Typically Cover
Daily or routine janitorial services for a standard office or commercial space usually include:
Restrooms (daily or multiple times daily in high-traffic environments):
- Restock paper towels, toilet paper, and hand soap
- Clean and disinfect toilets and urinals
- Clean sinks and mirrors
- Empty trash
- Mop floors
- Wipe high-touch surfaces (door handles, faucets, light switches)
Common areas and offices:
- Empty trash and recycling at every desk and workstation
- Vacuum carpeted areas
- Sweep and mop hard floors
- Wipe down conference tables, break room surfaces, and common areas
- Clean the break room kitchen area: wipe counters, clean sink, wipe appliance exteriors
- Restock break room supplies if applicable
Building entrances:
- Sweep and mop entryway floors
- Clean interior glass doors
- Empty entry trash receptacles
What janitorial services typically do not include: deep cleaning inside appliances, window washing (exterior), carpet cleaning, floor stripping and waxing, high-dusting above reach, cleaning behind equipment, or any significant periodic service beyond routine daily maintenance.

chunks.title: Blog: Commercial Cleaning vs. Janitorial Services: What Does Your Business Need?
chunks.section: What Commercial Deep Cleaning Typically Covers
chunks.text:
## What Commercial Deep Cleaning Typically Covers
A commercial deep cleaning session addresses what routine janitorial work accumulates over time. For most businesses, this is scheduled monthly, quarterly, or seasonally.
- High dusting: ceiling fans, light fixtures, vents, and surfaces above standard reach
- Deep restroom cleaning: scrubbing tile grout, descaling fixtures, cleaning behind toilets and under sinks
- Kitchen and break room deep clean: inside appliances, inside cabinets, behind and under equipment
- Window cleaning (interior)
- Carpet cleaning or extraction
- Hard floor deep cleaning, stripping, and refinishing where applicable
- Wiping all baseboards throughout the space
- Cleaning behind and under office furniture
- Cleaning HVAC vents and supply registers
Commercial cleaning is also used for specific situations: post-construction cleaning, move-in or move-out cleaning for commercial spaces, pre-event or post-event cleaning, and seasonal deep cleaning at the start or end of heavy business periods.

chunks.title: Blog: Commercial Cleaning vs. Janitorial Services: What Does Your Business Need?
chunks.section: Types of Businesses and What They Typically Need
chunks.text:
## Types of Businesses and What They Typically Need
The right cleaning structure varies significantly by business type.
## Small Offices (Under 2,000 sq ft, 5-15 employees)
Light daily or every-other-day janitorial is appropriate for most small offices. The restrooms and break room need regular attention. Individual offices and common areas can typically be maintained with less frequent cleaning if employees maintain reasonable tidiness at their workstations.
A monthly commercial deep cleaning handles the accumulated buildup that daily cleaning doesn’t reach. Many small offices opt for a weekly professional cleaning that combines the daily janitorial scope with more thorough attention, eliminating the need to separately manage both services.
## Medical and Healthcare Facilities
Healthcare environments have the most rigorous cleaning requirements. Cleaning protocols must address infection control and may need to meet specific regulatory standards. Daily janitorial is required, but with healthcare-specific disinfection protocols for patient areas, waiting rooms, restrooms, and exam rooms. Specialized cleaning companies with healthcare experience and the appropriate disinfectant certifications are necessary.

chunks.title: Blog: Commercial Cleaning vs. Janitorial Services: What Does Your Business Need?
chunks.text:
## Retail Spaces
Retail environments need daily maintenance cleaning (floors, restrooms, fitting rooms, surfaces) and periodic deep cleaning. High customer foot traffic means floors need more frequent attention. Fitting rooms require daily cleaning. Display surfaces need regular dusting.
## Restaurants and Food Service
Commercial kitchen cleaning is a specialized category. Food service facilities have specific health code requirements for grease trap cleaning, exhaust hood cleaning, equipment cleaning, and frequency of service. Restaurant cleaning is typically performed nightly after close and requires food-service-specific products and protocols.
## Warehouses and Industrial Spaces
Industrial facilities need floor maintenance (sweeping, mopping, or industrial scrubbing), restroom cleaning, and break room maintenance. High-dusting of shelving and equipment areas becomes more critical for facilities where dust accumulation is a fire or equipment hazard.
## Property Management (Apartments and Condos)
Property managers need turnover cleaning between tenants (equivalent to move-in/move-out cleaning), regular common area maintenance (hallways, lobbies, laundry rooms, amenity spaces), and periodic deep cleaning. chunks.text:
## Frequently Asked Questions
What is the difference between commercial cleaning and janitorial services?
Janitorial services cover routine daily or frequent maintenance cleaning: trash removal, restroom cleaning, floor sweeping, and surface wiping. Commercial cleaning refers to deeper periodic cleaning that addresses buildup, deep cleans surfaces, and covers areas that daily maintenance doesn’t reach. Many companies provide both under a combined service agreement.
How much does commercial cleaning cost in Minnesota?
For a small office of 1,000 to 2,000 square feet, expect $150 to $350 per routine cleaning visit. Deep cleaning sessions for the same space run $250 to $500. Pricing depends on the scope, frequency, and specific services included. A site visit from the cleaning company provides the most accurate quote.
How often should a business be professionally cleaned?
At minimum, restrooms and high-traffic common areas should be cleaned at least weekly. For offices with significant daily foot traffic, two to three times per week is more appropriate. Deep cleaning sessions are typically scheduled monthly or quarterly.
Do I need a contract for commercial cleaning services?

chunks.title: Blog: Commercial Cleaning vs. Janitorial Services: What Does Your Business Need?
chunks.text:
## Frequently Asked Questions (cont.)
Most commercial cleaning companies work under service agreements that define the scope, frequency, pricing, and cancellation terms. Review the agreement carefully before signing, particularly the cancellation terms and what constitutes the defined scope of service.
What’s included in a commercial cleaning contract?
The contract should specifically list every task included in each visit, the frequency of each task, the pricing structure, payment terms, the cancellation policy, and liability and insurance provisions. Anything not listed in the contract is not guaranteed to be included.
Is commercial cleaning tax deductible for businesses?
Yes. Commercial cleaning services for business premises are a deductible business expense. Consult a tax professional for guidance specific to your business structure.
How do I transition from an existing cleaning company?
Review your current contract’s cancellation clause for required notice periods (typically 30 days). Provide written notice within that window. Schedule your new service to begin when the old contract ends, and arrange for a walkthrough with the new company before their first visit to establish expectations.

## How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
Published/updated: 2026-07-16
Granite countertops are a valuable addition to many Twin Cities kitchens, but improper cleaning products can cause lasting damage. While many homeowners believe they’re caring for their countertops correctly, the real problem is often using cleaners that aren’t safe for natural stone.
Most households have granite-damaging products sitting right next to their granite countertops: white vinegar, lemon juice, bleach, and all-purpose cleaners with citrus extracts. These are some of the most popular general cleaning products available, and all of them damage granite over time, either by etching the stone itself or by degrading the sealant that protects it.
This guide covers what granite actually is and why it requires specific care, the safe daily cleaning routine, how to disinfect without causing damage, how to remove stains correctly based on the stain type, and how to seal and maintain granite so it stays in good condition for decades.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.section: Understanding Granite Before You Clean It
chunks.text:
## Understanding Granite Before You Clean It
Granite is a natural igneous rock formed from cooled magma. Its composition varies significantly from slab to slab, which is part of what makes each granite countertop visually unique. The primary minerals are quartz, feldspar, and mica, with varying amounts of other minerals depending on where the stone was quarried.
Because granite is a natural porous stone, liquid can penetrate the surface and cause staining. To prevent this, granite countertops are sealed with a penetrating stone sealer at installation and should be resealed periodically. The sealant fills the pores and creates a barrier against moisture and oils.
Here’s the critical point: both the granite itself and the sealant can be permanently damaged by the wrong cleaning products. The damage from acidic cleaners is called etching, which appears as dull spots or cloudiness on the surface. Etching damages the stone itself, not just the sealant, and cannot be reversed without professional polishing.
This is why granite care is different from cleaning any other kitchen surface.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.section: Products That Damage Granite (Never Use These)
chunks.text:
## Products That Damage Granite (Never Use These)
This list is more important than the cleaning steps themselves, because many of these products feel intuitively safe or natural.
Vinegar is acidic (pH around 2-3). It’s excellent for mineral deposits on faucets and shower glass. On granite, it etches the stone and degrades the sealant. A single cleaning won’t cause visible damage. Repeated use over months creates a permanently dull, hazed surface. White vinegar:
Same problem as vinegar. Citric acid etches granite. Products labeled as “natural” or “citrus-powered” are often particularly harmful to stone surfaces because they rely on citric acid as the active cleaning agent. Lemon juice and citrus-based cleaners:
Bleach doesn’t etch granite the way acids do, but it degrades the sealant, leaving the stone unprotected against staining. Repeated bleach use on granite countertops requires more frequent resealing and eventually causes the stone to become dull and porous-looking. Bleach and bleach-based cleaners:
Window cleaners like Windex contain ammonia, which damages granite sealant. Many all-purpose sprays also contain ammonia. Ammonia-based cleaners:
Pharmacy-strength 3% hydrogen peroxide is safe for occasional stain treatment on granite. Concentrated hydrogen peroxide products are not. Hydrogen peroxide (concentrated):

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.section: Products That Damage Granite (Never Use These)
chunks.text:
## Products That Damage Granite (Never Use These) (cont.)
Physically scratch the granite surface and sealant. Abrasive scrubbers and steel wool:
Most contain one or more of the above. Unless a product is specifically labeled as safe for natural stone, assume it’s not safe for granite. Generic all-purpose sprays:

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.text:
## Daily Granite Countertop Cleaning
Daily cleaning of granite countertops requires nothing more than warm water, a small amount of mild dish soap, and a microfiber cloth.
Add a few drops of mild dish soap to warm water (do not use a dish soap with citrus extracts or degreasing agents that contain citric acid). Dampen a microfiber cloth in the solution, wring out most of the water, and wipe the countertop surface. Rinse your cloth with clean water frequently so you’re not spreading soapy residue.
The crucial final step: dry the countertop thoroughly with a clean, dry microfiber cloth. Water left sitting on granite can leave hard water mineral spots, particularly in Minnesota’s hard water areas. The mineral deposits don’t damage the stone but they create a hazy appearance that requires additional effort to remove.
That’s the complete daily cleaning routine. Frequency matters more than effort: daily wiping prevents the buildup that requires more aggressive cleaning.
For a more effective daily spray, mix half a cup of rubbing alcohol, one teaspoon of mild dish soap, and one and a half cups of warm water in a spray bottle. Add a few drops of essential oil if desired. This cleans, sanitizes lightly, and is safe for granite sealant. Spray, wipe, and dry. DIY granite cleaner (safe version):

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.section: How to Disinfect Granite Countertops Safely
chunks.text:
## How to Disinfect Granite Countertops Safely
Dish soap and water clean and sanitize granite adequately for everyday kitchen use. When you handle raw meat or poultry on or near granite surfaces, more thorough disinfection is warranted.
The safe disinfectant for granite is isopropyl rubbing alcohol (70%). Mix equal parts 70% isopropyl alcohol and water in a spray bottle. Spray the countertop surface, let it sit for three to five minutes (dwell time kills bacteria), then wipe with a clean cloth and dry.
70% isopropyl alcohol is effective against bacteria and many viruses without damaging granite sealant. Higher concentrations (90%+) evaporate too quickly to disinfect effectively. Lower concentrations are less effective.
Do not use disinfecting wipes on granite. Most disinfecting wipes contain citric acid or other ingredients that damage granite sealant despite the wipes feeling gentle.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.section: How to Remove Stains From Granite Countertops
chunks.text:
## How to Remove Stains From Granite Countertops
Stain removal from granite depends entirely on what caused the stain. Using the wrong removal method can make the stain worse or cause additional damage.
First, understand the distinction between a stain and etching. A stain is discoloration from a substance that has absorbed into the stone. It will appear as a dark or differently colored area. An etch is damage to the stone surface caused by acid. It appears as a dull spot that feels different from the surrounding stone. Stains and etching require different approaches.
## Oil-Based Stains (Cooking Oil, Grease, Butter)
These appear as dark spots or spreading discoloration on granite. Oil has absorbed into the pores.
Make a paste of baking soda and water (for oil-based stains). Apply the paste to the stain and cover with plastic wrap. Tape the edges to create a seal. Leave for 24 to 48 hours. The paste draws the oil out of the stone as it dries. Wipe away the paste with a damp cloth. Repeat if the stain is not fully removed.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.text:
## Water-Based Stains (Coffee, Tea, Wine, Juice)
Make a paste of baking soda and hydrogen peroxide (3% from the pharmacy). Apply, cover with plastic wrap, and leave for 24 hours. The hydrogen peroxide helps lift organic staining without damaging the stone at pharmacy concentration. Wipe clean and repeat if needed.
## Hard Water Deposits (Minnesota-Specific)
Mineral deposits from hard water that build up on granite near the sink or faucet appear as white or grayish spots or haze. These are deposits on top of the stone, not stains that have absorbed in.
A small amount of granite-safe stone cleaner (such as StoneTech Professional or similar) handles mineral deposits on granite without the damage caused by vinegar. Do not use CLR, lime removers, or vinegar on granite for hard water deposits, despite these being the standard recommendation for hard water elsewhere in the home.
## Etching (Dull Spots From Acid Contact)
Etching is damage to the stone surface, not a stain. Marble polishing powder (available at stone care retailers) applied with a soft cloth and rubbed in circles can improve light etching. Deep etching requires professional polishing.
Prevention is more practical than repair for etching. Clean up any acidic liquid (citrus juice, wine, coffee, vinegar, tomato sauce) immediately. Don’t let acidic foods or liquids sit on the granite surface.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.section: How to Test if Your Granite Needs Resealing
chunks.text:
## How to Test if Your Granite Needs Resealing
Granite should be sealed at installation and resealed periodically. The resealing schedule depends on the stone’s porosity and the type of sealant used, typically every six months to three years.
The water test determines if resealing is needed: Leave a quarter cup of water on the granite surface for 15 minutes. If the water beads up and sits on the surface, the sealant is intact. If the water partially absorbs and leaves a dark spot, or if the spot remains damp after wiping, the sealant is depleted and the countertop needs resealing.
## How to Seal Granite Countertops
Purchase a penetrating stone sealer specifically formulated for granite (brands include StoneTech BulletProof, Miracle Sealants 511, or similar). Do not use surface sealers or topical treatments.
Clean and dry the countertop completely. Apply the sealer with a clean cloth in a thin, even coat. Let it penetrate for the time specified on the product label. Wipe away any excess before it dries. Allow to cure according to the product instructions before using the counter normally.
Annual sealing with a quality product is a straightforward maintenance task that significantly extends the life and appearance of granite countertops.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.section: Granite vs Other Stone Countertops: Cleaning Differences
chunks.text:
## Granite vs Other Stone Countertops: Cleaning Differences
Many Minnesota kitchens have stone countertops that are not granite, and the cleaning rules differ.
Engineered quartz (brands like Silestone, Caesarstone) is non-porous and doesn’t require sealing. It’s more resistant to staining and etching than natural granite. However, it can still be damaged by harsh chemicals and highly acidic cleaners. Mild soap and water or a pH-neutral cleaner is appropriate. Quartz countertops:
Much more sensitive to acid than granite. Etching happens very quickly from everyday kitchen acids (coffee, orange juice, tomato sauce). These stones require pH-neutral cleaners and immediate cleanup of any spills. Vinegar should never come near marble. Marble and limestone:
Non-porous, requires mineral oil treatment rather than sealing. More resistant to staining than granite. Soapstone:
Natural stone often confused with quartz. Requires the same care as granite: sealing, pH-neutral cleaners, no acidic products. Quartzite:

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.text:
## Frequently Asked Questions
What is the best cleaner for granite countertops?
Mild dish soap with warm water is best for daily cleaning. For disinfecting, equal parts 70% isopropyl alcohol and water. For stains, baking soda pastes with water (oil stains) or hydrogen peroxide (water-based stains). For everything else, a pH-neutral stone cleaner specifically formulated for granite.
Can I use vinegar to clean granite countertops?
No. Vinegar is acidic and etches granite, causing permanent dull spots and degrading the sealant. This is one of the most common mistakes homeowners make with granite. Despite being widely recommended as a natural cleaner, vinegar should never be used on any natural stone surface.
How do I remove hard water stains from granite?
Use a granite-safe stone cleaner rather than acidic products like CLR or vinegar. A paste of baking soda and water applied to the stain and left for 30 minutes can help with mineral deposits on the surface. Hard water deposits on granite require different treatment than hard water deposits on chrome or glass.
How often should granite countertops be sealed?
Perform the water test annually: if water absorbs within 15 minutes rather than beading up, reseal. Most granite needs resealing every one to three years depending on the stone and the type of sealer used.
Is it safe to prepare food directly on granite countertops?

chunks.title: Blog: How to Clean Granite Countertops: Safe Methods and Common Mistakes
chunks.text:
## Frequently Asked Questions (cont.)
Yes. Sealed granite is food-safe. However, granite is harder than most knife blades and will dull them quickly. Use a cutting board rather than cutting directly on the stone.
What’s the difference between etching and staining on granite?
A stain is dark discoloration from a substance absorbed into the stone. An etch is a dull spot caused by acid damaging the stone surface. Stains are addressed with drawing pastes. Etching requires polishing powder or professional restoration. Prevention through immediate spill cleanup is more practical than either repair.
Can you use disinfecting wipes on granite?
No. Most disinfecting wipes contain citric acid or other ingredients that damage granite sealant despite their gentle feel. Use the alcohol and water solution described above for disinfecting.

## Protect Your Granite Investment
Granite countertops cleaned and maintained properly look beautiful for decades. The key is knowing which products to avoid and building a simple daily routine with the right ones.

chunks.section: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.text:
## How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
Published/updated: 2026-11-12
Shower mold has a habit of coming back. You scrub it off, it looks clean for a week, and then it’s back in the same spots. Most people treat the visible symptom without addressing what’s actually causing it, which is why the problem keeps repeating.
Removing shower mold properly requires understanding what type of mold you’re dealing with, using the right product for the surface it’s on, allowing enough dwell time for the cleaning agent to work, and then changing the conditions that allowed mold to establish itself in the first place.
This guide covers all of it, including the specific techniques that work on different surfaces in the shower, why mold keeps coming back in certain areas, how to tell when the problem is beyond surface cleaning, and what to do about persistent mold in a Minnesota home where humidity management has its own seasonal challenges.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: What Is Shower Mold and Why Does It Grow There?
chunks.text:
## What Is Shower Mold and Why Does It Grow There?
Mold is a fungus that grows wherever three conditions are present simultaneously: moisture, organic material to feed on, and relatively still air. Showers provide all three. Water is present constantly. Soap residue, skin cells, and body oils provide organic material. Steam creates warm, moist air that doesn’t circulate well in enclosed shower spaces.
The most common types of shower mold are Cladosporium, Penicillium, and Aspergillus. These appear as black, gray, or greenish discoloration on grout, caulk, tile, and shower surfaces. They’re the molds that respond to proper cleaning. Stachybotrys chartarum, commonly called black mold, grows under different conditions (sustained heavy moisture from leaks or flooding) and is less common in shower surfaces.
Understanding this distinction matters: the dark mold on your shower grout is almost certainly a common surface mold, not the hazardous variety that makes the news. But it’s still worth eliminating promptly, because it affects air quality and indicates moisture management issues that can lead to bigger structural problems over time.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: Identifying Where Shower Mold Is Growing
chunks.text:
## Identifying Where Shower Mold Is Growing
Before choosing a cleaning approach, identify exactly where the mold is:
The most common location. Grout is porous and absorbs moisture and soap residue, creating ideal mold conditions below the surface. Surface cleaning alone doesn’t reach the mold roots in porous grout. Grout lines:
Mold in caulk penetrates the material itself. If the caulk is turning black or gray and cleaning doesn’t clear it, the mold has gone into the caulk, not just onto it. Caulk around the tub or shower base:
Non-porous tile is the easiest surface to clean. Surface mold on tile responds quickly to most cleaning agents. Tile surface:
These collect standing water and soap residue and are frequently neglected. Dark buildup in the tracks is usually a combination of mold and soap scum. Shower door tracks and frames:
Mold on the ceiling indicates that steam is rising and condensing there without adequate ventilation. This is a ventilation problem, not just a cleaning problem. Shower ceiling:
If mold keeps returning very rapidly (within days) despite cleaning, or if there’s a persistent musty smell even after cleaning, mold may be growing behind the tile where water has penetrated through failed grout or caulk. This requires professional assessment. Behind tiles or in wall cavities:

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: What You Need Before You Start
chunks.text:
## What You Need Before You Start
Gather supplies before you begin. Working with mold cleaning products requires respiratory protection.
- N-95 respirator mask (not just a cloth mask)
- Safety glasses
- Rubber gloves
- Stiff-bristled grout brush and an old toothbrush
- Spray bottle
- White distilled vinegar
- Hydrogen peroxide (3%)
- Oxygen bleach (OxiClean or similar)
- Chlorine bleach (for white grout only, not colored grout)
- Baking soda
- Microfiber cloths
- Ventilation: open the bathroom window and run the exhaust fan
Never mix bleach with vinegar, ammonia, or any other cleaner. The combination produces toxic chloramine gas. Use one product at a time, rinsing thoroughly between applications if switching.
## How to Remove Mold From Shower Grout
Grout is the most challenging surface because mold penetrates the porous material rather than just sitting on top.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: Method 1: Hydrogen Peroxide (Best for Most Shower Grout)
chunks.text:
## Method 1: Hydrogen Peroxide (Best for Most Shower Grout)
Hydrogen peroxide kills mold at the root level, penetrates porous grout better than bleach, and doesn’t produce harsh fumes. It’s the best starting point for most shower grout mold.
Apply 3% hydrogen peroxide directly to the moldy grout with a spray bottle. Do not dilute it. Let it sit for 15 to 20 minutes. The dwell time is critical. Spraying and immediately wiping distributes mold spores without killing them.
After 15 to 20 minutes, scrub the grout lines with a stiff grout brush, working along the grout line direction. Rinse thoroughly with warm water. For heavy mold, repeat the application.
## Method 2: Baking Soda and Hydrogen Peroxide Paste (For Heavy Mold)
Mix hydrogen peroxide and baking soda into a paste. Apply the paste to moldy grout lines and press it into the grout with a brush. Let it sit for 20 to 30 minutes. Scrub with a grout brush and rinse completely.
The baking soda acts as a mild abrasive that helps lift embedded mold from the grout surface while the hydrogen peroxide kills the mold at depth.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.text:
## Method 3: Oxygen Bleach (For Stubborn Staining)
OxiClean or similar oxygen bleach products are effective on heavily stained white or light grout. Mix to a thick paste with a small amount of water. Apply to grout, cover with plastic wrap to prevent drying, and leave for 30 to 60 minutes. Scrub and rinse.
Oxygen bleach is safe on colored grout, unlike chlorine bleach. It’s the strongest effective option that doesn’t risk discoloring your grout.
## Method 4: Chlorine Bleach (For White Grout Only, Heavy Mold)
For white grout with severe, established mold staining, a diluted bleach solution (one part bleach to ten parts water) applied with a brush and left for 10 to 15 minutes is effective. Rinse completely and ventilate the bathroom well.
Never use chlorine bleach on colored, tan, or gray grout. It will permanently discolor or bleach the grout unevenly.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: How to Remove Mold From Shower Caulk
chunks.text:
## How to Remove Mold From Shower Caulk
This is the most commonly misunderstood situation. If mold has penetrated the caulk itself, cleaning products won’t solve the problem permanently. They clean the surface, the mold regrows from inside the caulk within weeks, and the cycle repeats.
For light surface mold on caulk that hasn’t penetrated deeply: Apply hydrogen peroxide directly and let dwell for 20 minutes. Scrub with an old toothbrush. This works when the mold is recent and hasn’t embedded itself in the caulk material.
For established mold in caulk: Remove the caulk entirely using a caulk removal tool or a utility knife. Remove every trace of the old caulk and allow the joint to dry completely, at least 24 to 48 hours. Apply new mold-resistant caulk (it contains an antifungal agent) and allow it to cure fully before exposing to water.
Recaulking is the permanent solution for moldy caulk. Cleaning is a temporary fix that will need repeating.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: How to Remove Mold From Shower Tiles
chunks.text:
## How to Remove Mold From Shower Tiles
Tile is non-porous and the easiest shower surface to clean. Mold on tile surface typically responds quickly to standard cleaning agents.
Spray with white vinegar or hydrogen peroxide. Let sit for 10 to 15 minutes. Wipe clean with a microfiber cloth and rinse.
For natural stone tile (marble, travertine, limestone): Never use vinegar or any acid-based product. These permanently etch and damage natural stone. Use a pH-neutral tile cleaner or hydrogen peroxide on natural stone only.
For the shower door glass and tracks: Apply undiluted white vinegar to glass, let sit 15 minutes, scrub with a non-scratch sponge and rinse. For the tracks, use an old toothbrush and the same vinegar solution. Rinse and dry the tracks completely after cleaning.
## How to Remove Mold From the Shower Ceiling
Mold on the shower ceiling requires extra care because working overhead with cleaning solutions creates drip and splash hazards.
Apply hydrogen peroxide using a sponge on a long handle rather than a spray bottle. Let dwell for 15 minutes. Scrub with a brush attached to an extension pole and rinse.
Shower ceiling mold is a reliable indicator of inadequate ventilation. Cleaning it repeatedly without addressing ventilation is a losing battle. See the prevention section below.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: Why Shower Mold Keeps Coming Back
chunks.text:
## Why Shower Mold Keeps Coming Back
If mold returns consistently in the same spots within days or weeks of cleaning, one of these causes is usually responsible.
The exhaust fan isn’t running long enough, isn’t sized adequately for the bathroom, or isn’t venting properly (some fans vent into the attic rather than outside, which spreads moisture and can cause structural damage). The fan should run during and for at least 20 minutes after every shower. Inadequate ventilation:
Water is penetrating behind the tile or shower base through cracked caulk or deteriorating grout. This creates moisture in the wall cavity where mold grows in conditions you can’t see or reach with cleaning products. Signs include mold returning very quickly, soft or soft-feeling wall sections near the shower, or a persistent musty smell even after thorough cleaning. Caulk or grout failure:
Steam and water remaining on shower surfaces after each use constantly refreshes the moisture supply mold needs. See prevention steps below. Inadequate moisture removal after showering:
Some cleaning products kill surface mold but don’t penetrate grout deeply enough. Switching from a surface cleaner to hydrogen peroxide or oxygen bleach on porous grout often resolves the reoccurrence issue. Product sensitivity:
Seeing mold outside the bathroom too? Read our guide on. how to clean mold in your home safely

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: How to Prevent Shower Mold From Returning
chunks.text:
## How to Prevent Shower Mold From Returning
Cleaning shower mold thoroughly is step one. Preventing its return requires changing the moisture conditions in the bathroom.
During every shower and for 20 minutes afterward. If your bathroom has no exhaust fan or a weak one, this is the single most impactful improvement you can make. Run the exhaust fan properly.
This takes 30 seconds and removes most of the water before it can evaporate and maintain the moisture that mold needs. A shower squeegee kept inside the shower removes this friction. Squeegee shower walls and glass after every use.
Closing the shower immediately after use traps humidity inside, extending the moist period. Leaving it open allows airflow that dries surfaces faster. Leave the shower door or curtain open after showering.
Clean, dry grout treated with a penetrating grout sealer is significantly less porous and absorbs less moisture and soap residue. Sealed grout resists mold much more effectively than unsealed grout. Reapply annually. Apply a grout sealer after cleaning.
Spraying shower surfaces with a diluted hydrogen peroxide solution or a commercial daily shower spray after each use inhibits mold growth between cleaning sessions. Takes 15 seconds. Use a daily shower spray.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: How to Prevent Shower Mold From Returning
chunks.text:
## How to Prevent Shower Mold From Returning (cont.)
Any crack in caulk or deterioration in grout that allows water to penetrate behind the tile is a mold factory in the wall cavity. Recaulk and regrout as needed. Fix caulk and grout failures promptly.

## Minnesota-Specific Shower Mold Considerations
Minnesota’s climate creates specific bathroom moisture challenges.
During winter, homes are sealed for months with minimal fresh air exchange. Indoor humidity from cooking, bathing, and breathing has nowhere to escape. Bathrooms that may dry out adequately in more temperate climates during winter stay persistently damp in Minnesota homes.
HVAC systems during heating season dry the air significantly, but that dry air doesn’t reach inside shower enclosures effectively. The result is that shower surfaces stay moist longer between uses during Minnesota winters.
Running the exhaust fan consistently and using a bathroom humidity monitor (available for under $20 at any hardware store) helps. If bathroom humidity consistently exceeds 60 percent between showers, additional ventilation is warranted.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.section: When to Call a Professional Cleaning Service
chunks.text:
## When to Call a Professional Cleaning Service
Surface shower mold that hasn’t returned rapidly is manageable with the steps in this guide. Professional bathroom cleaning makes sense when:
The mold is extensive and covers large grout areas that would require hours of hand scrubbing. A professional team completes this work in a fraction of the time with commercial-grade products.
The bathroom needs a full deep clean, not just mold treatment. Our covers grout, caulk, tile, and every other bathroom surface in a single professional visit. deep cleaning service

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.text:
## Frequently Asked Questions
What kills mold in a shower?
Hydrogen peroxide (3%), oxygen bleach (OxiClean), and chlorine bleach (for white grout only) all effectively kill shower mold. Hydrogen peroxide is the most versatile option: it kills mold, penetrates porous grout, is safe on most colored surfaces, and doesn’t produce harsh fumes. Dwell time of 15 to 20 minutes is essential.
Does vinegar kill shower mold?
White vinegar kills approximately 82 percent of mold species and is effective on light shower mold, particularly on non-porous surfaces. It penetrates grout better than bleach. For established or heavy mold in grout, hydrogen peroxide or oxygen bleach is more effective. Never use vinegar on natural stone tile.
Why does mold keep coming back in my shower?
The most common causes are insufficient ventilation (the exhaust fan isn’t running long enough or isn’t sized properly), mold penetrating the caulk rather than just sitting on the surface (requiring caulk replacement), or grout and caulk failures allowing water to reach wall cavities. Addressing the root cause is necessary to stop recurrence.
Is shower mold dangerous?

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.text:
## Frequently Asked Questions (cont.)
Common shower surface molds (Cladosporium, Penicillium, Aspergillus) are typically irritating rather than hazardous for healthy adults. They can worsen respiratory conditions and cause allergic reactions. If you suspect a more serious mold type due to significant water damage or rapid reoccurrence, contact a mold remediation professional for testing and assessment.
How do I know if mold is in my shower walls?
Signs of mold in wall cavities behind shower tile include mold returning within days of cleaning, soft or spongy tile or wall sections, peeling grout or caulk, and a persistent musty smell even after thorough cleaning. This requires professional assessment, not DIY cleaning.
How long does it take to remove shower mold?
A single shower treated with hydrogen peroxide and scrubbed properly takes 45 to 90 minutes. Extensive mold on multiple grout surfaces takes longer. Professional cleaning teams complete the work faster with commercial equipment.
Can I use a steam cleaner to remove shower mold?
Yes. Steam cleaning at high temperatures kills mold effectively on tile and non-porous surfaces and is chemical-free. It’s less effective on deep grout mold compared to hydrogen peroxide with dwell time, but it’s a good option for regular maintenance cleaning and for households preferring to avoid chemicals.

chunks.title: Blog: How to Remove Shower Mold (And Keep It From Coming Back)
chunks.text:
## Get Your Shower Properly Clean
Removing shower mold thoroughly and preventing its return is a realistic goal with the right approach. The key is using the right product for the specific surface, giving it enough time to work, and then changing the moisture conditions that allowed mold to establish.
